To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the crustal response of NW Europe to deglaciation of the Fennos-candian ice sheet is well constrained by the inversion of Late Quaternary sea-level observations and (ii) this crustal response is consistent with a total volume of ice of 13-14m equivalent sea-level rise in the Fennos-scandian ice sheet, and 10 m equivalent in the BarentsKara ice sheet.

the Earth’s response to the deglaciations and to the melting of ice sheets in the past is described by a mantle viscosity that is about 2-4 times larger than that of a standard Earth model, the lithosphere is thicker than the standard model and the mantle is more viscous below about 700 km depth than above.

the Earth’s response to surface loading by ice sheets and by water is characterized by an increase in viscosity from upper to lower mantles and a thick lithosphere, and that a significant proportion of sea-level rise during Late Holocene times has been contributed from ice sheets outside Europe.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the reconstruction of sea-level change and crustal deformation in NW Europe during Late Pleistocene to Holocene times.
the reconstruction of past ice-sheet configurations from the geological record.
the reconstruction of the history of the Earth’s surface from geological observations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the total equivalent sea-level rise since the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) was about 26 m. The total equivalent sea-level drop during glaciation was 120-130 m.
the crustal response of the Earth is consistent with a model of mantle viscosity of (3-5). X 10’’’Pa s in the upper mantle and of (2-7). X loz’ Pa s in the lower mantle.
the total equivalent sea-level rise due to deglaciation of all ice sheets during the past 20,000 yr was about 30 m, and that the equivalent sea level rise during the last 6000 yr was about 10 m.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Earth’s response to the deglaciations of the Late Quaternary was dominated by the response of the Fennoscanian ice sheet.

the crustal response to Late Holocene loading has been very complex and has involved a combination of elastic, visco-elastic and viscous processes in the upper mantle and lithosphere and viscous processes within the lower mantle.

the Earth’s crust has been responding to the deglaciated Fennoscandic and Barents-Karic ice sheets for the past 12 000 yr and that it will continue to do so for at least the next 10 000 yr, but that this response is not a simple elastic one and that there is no evidence for a major change in the rate of response during the Late Holocene.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, for any particular region, the crustal response to ice loading and unloading is highly variable and that this variability must be taken into account when considering the effects of climate change on the Earth’s crust.

the Earth’s response to the deglaciations of Fennoscandinavia, the British-Irish Ice Sheet and the Laurentide Ice Sheet has been a major factor in the sea-level changes observed during the Late Pleistocene.

the crustal response to deglaciation of the Fennos-candian ice sheet is very sensitive to the ice models that are used to drive the inversion, and that the resulting mantle parameters are also sensitive to the ice model.
